item.title: Imperial Oil CEO optimistic on progress toward firming up Pathways agreement
item.description: The chief executive of Imperial Oil Ltd. says he’s encouraged by progress made toward pinning down a final agreement with the federal and Alberta governments to advance the Pathways carbon storage ...
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: The chief executive of Imperial Oil Ltd. says he’s encouraged by progress made toward pinning down a final agreement with the federal and Alberta governments to advance the Pathways carbon storage project, which is a condition for the Pacific Link crude pipeline to the West Coast moving ahead. Members of the Oil Sands Alliance, which includes Imperial and four of its peers, reached a non-binding memorandum of understanding with Ottawa and the province in July. They set a Nov. 15 target to finalize binding agreements with each of the companies. “There’s still a lot of work left to do. That’s only a couple of weeks away, but there’s no lack of energy or desire to get to a definitive agreement,” Imperial CEO John Whelan told analysts on a conference call Friday to discuss third-quarter results. “We’re going to make sure we do all the right things that enable us to execute on the definitive agreement. So most importantly is, for me, the shared ambition to make this happen and the work that’s going into that. And I remain really encouraged about where we are.” The Pathways-pipeline quid pro quo was part of a sweeping accord Ottawa and Alberta signed in November 2025 on a wide array of energy matters. The idea is for Pathways to offset some of the carbon dioxide emissions that Pacific Link, recently deemed by Ottawa a project in the national interest, would enable through increased oilsands production. Pathways involves a pipeline network that would carry carbon dioxide captured from various oilsands sites in northern Alberta to an underground storage hub near Cold Lake, Alta. The alliance said that the Pathways Project will have the capacity to transport and store about six million tonnes per year of captured CO2 by the mid-2030s. The parties are aiming for another 10 million tonnes of reductions by 2045. That’s a significant scale-back from the 22 million tonnes of emissions by 2030 they had earlier targeted. In the July Pathways-centred MOU, governments agreed to pursue regulatory and fiscal policies that would spur oilsands growth, which in turn would ensure the pipeline from Alberta to a tanker port in southern British Columbia can be filled. Ottawa agreed to extending investment tax credits for certain carbon-capture equipment, while Alberta has agreed to “financial supports” to encourage oilsands growth, alluding recently to potential royalty incentives. The other Oil Sands Alliance members are Suncor Energy, Canadian Natural Resources, Cenovus Energy and ConocoPhillips. Earlier Friday, Imperial reported a third-quarter profit of $2.45 billion, up from $539 million in the same quarter last year, boosted by higher oil prices. The profit amounted to $5.11 per diluted share for the quarter compared with a profit of $1.07 per diluted share a year ago. Total revenue and other income amounted to $16.21 billion, up from $12.05 billion in the same quarter last year. Upstream production averaged 418,000 gross oil-equivalent barrels per day, down from 462,000 a year ago, primarily due to lower production at Kearl and planned maintenance turnarounds at Cold Lake and Syncrude. Production in the oilsands was crimped by a third-party pipeline outage caused by an electrical transformer failure in mid-September, Whelan said. “We don’t see systemic issues. We see one-offs that we’re going to learn from,” he said. “We see nothing in the underlying performance that causes us any doubt whatsoever on our future targets.” Refinery throughput averaged 381,000 barrels per day, down from 425,000 in the third quarter of 2025 as capacity utilization dropped to 88 per cent, compared with 98 per cent in the third quarter of 2025. Imperial says it faced unplanned downtime, also due to a third-party pipeline outage. The price of West Texas Intermediate, the U.S. light oil benchmark, averaged US$85.68 during the third quarter, up from US$64.97 during the same period a year earlier. Western Canada Select, the price of heavy crude produced in Alberta, rose to US$71.90 from US$54.62 year-over-year during the quarter. In recent weeks the price gap between WTI and WCS has reportedly widened by as much as US$30, where normally it would be less than half that. Even so, Whelan said the market conditions are favourable for heavy oil producers like Imperial, which can make money and pay dividends at a price much lower than it is currently. “The absolute price of WCS remains extremely constructive.” This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 30, 2026. By Lauren Krugel

item.title: ‘Nice balancing point’: TMX CEO on the firm’s diversification efforts
item.description: The head of Toronto Stock Exchange (TSX) operator TMX Group Ltd. says the company has continued to diversify its global business offerings as it leans into data services and subscription models that ...
item.dc:creator: Jordan Fleguel
item.content:encoded: The head of Toronto Stock Exchange (TSX) operator TMX Group Ltd. says the company has continued to diversify its global business offerings as it leans into data services and subscription models that provide recurring revenue and stability. TMX CEO John McKenzie told BNN Bloomberg on Friday that the exchange operator has identified three strategic measures that make up its long-term diversification strategy. “One is around the global distribution, so we are now half of the business outside of Canada, half inside, and that’s a real nice balancing point for us,” he said. “It gives us access to the world, access to global investors, but it doesn’t reduce the prominence and importance of what we do in the Canadian market.” The second focus area, McKenzie said, involves its recurring revenue model, driven by the firm’s financial services that are subscription oriented. He said the company now brings in over 50 per cent of its revenue from subscriptions. “That gives investors a lot of confidence in the stability of the long-term growth of the organization, as opposed to what can happen on a cyclical basis,” said McKenzie. “But the last piece is around the real global insights in the data space… that’s now over 40 per cent of the franchise, and our objective is for that to be 50 per cent of the franchise, because it gives the organization way better balance.” TMX Group’s Q3 earnings TMX’s diversification strategy has been paying off for investors, McKenzie argued. His comments came a day after the company reported third quarter earnings that showed revenue grew by 17 per cent year-over-year. The firm reported adjusted diluted earnings per share of $0.63, up 21 per cent from the same quarter in 2025. “Organic revenue increased 11 per cent year-over-year, highlighted by double-digit growth in revenue from TMX VettaFi, Derivatives Trading and Clearing, and Capital Formation,” David Arnold, TMX’s chief financial officer, said in the company’s earnings release. “In addition to impressive business performance and excellent results, we advanced our long-term growth strategy by completing the acquisitions of Cboe Australia and RAFI Indices, funded with cash and debt. Our balance sheet is strong, and we remain agile in our investment approach.” McKenzie noted that those acquisitions led to a decrease in year-over-year net income in the quarter, but the transactions are designed to be “immediately accretive” for TMX investors. “Every acquisition we’ve done has been designed not just to create value for the shareholders, but also to create value for the Canadian ecosystem too,” he said. TMX has tapped debt markets in recent months to cover its acquisition costs. In September, it closed a $1.1 billion Canadian private placement debenture offering, and the company still has two acquisitions yet to close, McKenzie said. “But even when we get all this done, our total leverage in the organization… would be kind of about 3.2 times, which is a range we’ve been in before,” he said. “We’ve got a really good track record on pay down to get back to our target range of one and a half to two and a half (times), so it gives us the capabilities of continuing to deploy capital strategically if the right opportunity presents itself that helps to accelerate our strategy.” Listing challenges TMX Group’s focus on diversification comes at a time when fewer companies are being listed on Canada’s main stock exchange. The Canadian Press reported on Tuesday that during the first nine months of this year, there were 337 new listings on the TSX and its junior venture exchange, according to TMX’s September market intelligence report. Of those, only 101 were companies, with the others being investment products like exchange-traded funds (ETFs). During the same period five years ago, the number of total listings was comparable at 338, but 176 were companies. Earlier this week at a conference hosted by the Alberta Securities Commission, McKenzie said he’d like to see reduced regulatory barriers and cost relief for companies looking to go public on the TSX. The exchange has increasingly become home to “fewer, bigger companies, which in some ways is great,” he said, noting that larger firms are better able to compete globally. “But at the same time, if we hollow out that middle of the market, it makes it more difficult for small, big-cap companies to find the capital they need to scale up to become the next Enbridge or Shopify or RBC,” McKenzie told the conference. “We want to make sure that the ecosystem still exists.” With files from The Canadian Press

item.title: The sell-off for tech stocks deepens and drags Wall Street toward its worst day since June
item.description: A sell-off for tech stocks is getting worse Friday on worries that Wall Street’s frenzy around AI sent prices too high.
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.content:encoded: NEW YORK — A sell-off for tech stocks is getting worse Friday on worries that Wall Street’s frenzy around AI sent prices too high. The S&P 500 dropped 1.8 per cent and was on track to erase its gain for October, even though it set its all-time high during the month. The Nasdaq composite was likewise heading toward its worst day since June, as the weakness for technology stocks dragged it down three per cent, as of 12:55 p.m. Eastern time. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 496 points, or 0.9 per cent. Intel’s stock led the way downward and is flirting with its worst day since 1974 after tumbling 30.1 per cent. The chipmaker gave a forecast for profit in the final three months of this year that fell short of analysts’ expectations, as CEO Lip-Bu Tan said the personal-computer industry continues to feel pressure. The drop came even though Intel reported a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Amazon sank 2.3 per cent after reporting a weaker profit for the summer than analysts expected. Potentially more concerning for investors was Amazon’s reporting that it burned through US$42.4 billion of cash over the prior 12 months, according to a measure called free cash flow. It spent $94.8 billion on property and equipment, primarily through investments in artificial-intelligence technology. A day earlier, Alphabet’s stock dropped more than 12 per cent to its worst day on record and almost single-handedly dragged the S&P 500 lower after telling investors it burned through more cash during the summer than the spring. The company behind Google and YouTube cited similar, mammoth investments in AI. Worries are rising about whether all those hundreds of billions of dollars will produce enough profit and productivity to make the investment worth it. At the same time, stocks of computer chip companies and other winners from the frenzy to build AI data centers have come under pressure on concerns that high interest rates may slow the further build out of data centers. “We’re moving out of the hopes and dreams phase of the AI trade and into the ‘show me’ phase,” said Joe Tigay, portfolio manager at Equity Armor Investments, in a note to investors. A drop of 4.7 per cent for the stock price of Nvidia, whose chips have made it the poster child of the AI frenzy, was the heaviest force pulling the S&P 500 downward, even more than Intel. In the cryptocurrency industry, meanwhile, stocks tumbled following a hack on the world’s biggest crypto exchange. The price of bitcoin fell toward $77,000 from more than $86,000 earlier this month, and a U.S.-based blockchain intelligence firm said a North Korean unit was likely behind the attack that impacted more than $6 billion worth of crypto at Binance. Coinbase Global fell 12.9 per cent even though it reported stronger results for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Strategy, which says it owns about four per cent of the total supply of bitcoin, fell six per cent. It also reported a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected, while saying its chief financial officer will resign next week for personal reasons. Outside of tech, stocks were more resilient as many rallied after reporting stronger profits for the summer than analysts expected. Nearly as many stocks rose in the S&P 500 index as fell. ExxonMobil climbed 1.8 per cent, and Chevron added 1.6 per cent after the oil giants both reported stronger profit for the summer than analysts expected. Mondelez International rose 3.7 per cent after the company behind Oreo cookies and Ritz crackers reported stronger-than-expected growth. Colgate-Palmolive climbed 3.5 per cent after higher prices for its products around much of the world helped it deliver better revenue and profit than analysts expected. Expectations are high for U.S. companies’ ability to make bigger profits, even though people around the world are feeling discouraged about high inflation and high fuel prices. Such expectations are what drove the S&P 500 to its record earlier this month. In the bond market, Treasury yields eased in a signal that investors were buying U.S. government bonds in search of something safer to own. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.94 per cent from 4.98 per cent late Thursday and from more than 5.30 per cent earlier this month. Treasury yields fell even though oil prices bounced higher, something that usually drives yields higher because it worsens inflation. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil rose 2.4 per cent to $113.50. It’s near the high end of its range since the war with Iran sent oil prices and inflation higher. In stock markets abroad, indexes were mostly lower in Europe following sharper swings in Asia. South Korea’s Kospi dropped 3.5 per cent as worries about AI hit its tech-heavy market, while the Hang Seng in Hong Kong climbed 1.5 per cent. Japan’s Nikkei 225 fell 2.1 per cent after the Bank of Japan decided to keep interest rates steady, echoing moves made earlier in the week by the U.S. Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank. ___ AP Business Writers Yuri Kageyama and Michelle Chapman contributed to this report. By Stan Choe

item.title: Economic growth stalled again in August, StatCan says
item.description: Statistics Canada says the economy stalled for a second month in a row in August, and early estimates suggest growth declined in September.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: Signs that economic growth stalled over the summer have some economists debating the timing of the Bank of Canada’s next interest rate hike. Statistics Canada said Friday that real gross domestic product was essentially unchanged for a second straight month in August. That fell short of economists’ calls and the agency’s own early expectations for a gain of 0.2 per cent in the month. Wholesale trade fell 1.4 per cent in August as most subsectors contracted. StatCan said motor vehicle and vehicle parts wholesalers faced their first decline in seven months amid lower vehicle imports and weaker manufacturing activity in the subsector. StatCan cited a “prolonged summer shutdown at a major auto assembly plant” to explain a 5.8 per cent decline in motor vehicles and parts manufacturing in August. Tu Nguyen, chief economist at RSM Canada, said what’s notable about the August declines in these sectors is they would only partially capture the impacts of a breakdown in trade talks between Canada and the United States that month. Both sides have since levied new waves of tariffs and trade restrictions against one another. Manufacturing and wholesale trade — sectors that are particularly vulnerable to tariff disruptions — will continue to see regular contractions under the re-escalated trade dispute, Nguyen said. Elsewhere, StatCan said work to prepare the 2026 census was still winding down in August, driving widespread contractions in public administration. Maintenance work at some nuclear power plants and mining facilities in northern Alberta also dragged on growth that month, StatCan said. Retail trade, manufacturing as a whole and the transportation and warehousing industries were among those posting gains to offset the declines in August. StatCan’s early estimates for September suggest real GDP declined 0.1 per cent, driven by losses in manufacturing and mining, quarrying and oil and gas extraction. The agency’s flash estimates still see real GDP expanding 1.3 per cent on an annualized basis in the third quarter, a slowdown from 3.3 per cent growth in the second quarter. StatCan will provide its official quarterly estimates for the third quarter next month when it reports the September GDP figures. BMO chief economist Doug Porter said in a note to clients Friday that some of the weakness last quarter might be overstated, particularly as it relates to census-related slowdowns. “Still, with the trade tiff still flaring, housing struggling, and recent employment figures concerning, it certainly appears that growth has run into some pretty serious headwinds of late,” he said. The latest economic data comes two days after the Bank of Canada raised its benchmark interest rate by a quarter point to 2.5 per cent, the first hike in more than three years. An increase to the central bank’s key rate will typically take some steam out of the economy, though most analysts still see current monetary policy levels as somewhat stimulative. Officials at the central bank argued this week that a rate hike was warranted to get ahead of looming inflation risks. Governor Tiff Macklem pointed to signs of resilience in the Canadian economy over the spring in justifying the decision. The central bank also revised up its expectations for growth on Wednesday. Monetary policymakers are expecting growth in the third quarter ended up at two per cent on an annualized basis, up from 1.5 per cent in its July forecasts. Many economists weighing in Friday argued the Bank of Canada’s somewhat rosier projections are at risk after StatCan data suggested middling growth in the third quarter. BMO, which had been in line with the central bank’s call for two per cent growth, trimmed its outlook to 1.5 per cent after Friday’s surprise. The Bank of Canada is expecting a further slowdown in the fourth quarter will give way to real GDP growth of two per cent in 2027 and 2028. Nguyen said despite the recent stumbles, there are reasons for optimism in the year ahead. Government spending priorities for a build out of major projects and tax incentives for business investment should give the economy a lift in 2027, she argued. Andrew Grantham, senior economist at CIBC, said in a note that the August data suggested the economy “was already struggling for momentum even before this week’s interest rate hike.” A slower-than-expected economy could help relieve inflationary pressures and reduce the need for additional rate hikes, he added. The weak GDP results support a pause from the Bank of Canada at its final rate decision of the year in December, Grantham said, though he noted there’s plenty of additional economic data to come before that meeting. Financial market odds of an interest rate hike on Dec. 9 stood at 57 per cent as of Friday morning, according to LSEG Data & Analytics. Nguyen said it’s a “coin flip” whether the Bank of Canada hikes in December or its next meeting in January. But given Macklem’s comments this week focused on economic resilience and inflationary fears, she said she leans toward a second quarter-point hike sooner than later. “A 25-basis-point hike, one month apart, whether in December or in January, I don’t think would change too much in terms of growth trajectory,” she said. This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 30, 2026. By Craig Lord
